FREEZING YOUR EGGS IN YOUR 30s

Fertility planning is becoming an important topic for many women, but decisions around egg freezing are often influenced by trends, online information, and individual circumstances.

Some important considerations include:

• Fertility potential may change with age
• Egg number and egg quality are both important factors in fertility discussions
• Conditions such as PCOS and Endometriosis can affect fertility experiences differently from person to person
• Previous ovarian procedures or medical history may be relevant in fertility planning
• Egg freezing is one option that may be considered as part of a broader fertility strategy

For some women, fertility preservation may be an option worth discussing. For others, timing and individual circumstances may differ.

Factors that may be considered include:

• age
• ovarian reserve assessment
• family planning goals
• relationship timelines
• medical history
• emotional and financial considerations

The focus should be on informed decision-making and understanding available options.

If you are considering fertility preservation, a discussion may include realistic expectations, fertility planning, and individualized guidance.

— Dr. Latika Chawla
Gynecological Endoscopic & Endometriosis Surgeon

Pelvic pain in Endometriosis can sometimes involve more than active disease alone.

For some women, ongoing discomfort may be influenced by multiple factors, including inflammation, tissue changes, muscle tension, movement patterns, and how the nervous system processes pain signals over time.

Adhesions are bands of scar tissue that may develop after inflammation, surgery, or disease processes. In some cases, they may affect how tissues and organs move in relation to one another.

Some women may experience symptoms such as:

• pelvic discomfort
• stiffness or restricted movement
• muscle tension
• increased sensitivity to pain
• reduced confidence with movement due to discomfort

Every experience can be different, and symptoms do not always correlate directly with the amount of visible disease.

This is one reason why endometriosis care often extends beyond treatment of disease alone and may also focus on overall function, movement, symptom management, and quality of life.

If pelvic symptoms continue after treatment or surgery, discussing them with your healthcare professional may help guide further evaluation.

Can having fewer periods extend fertility?

There has been recent discussion around fertility research and whether changes in menstrual patterns could one day influence reproductive aging.

Here’s the important context:

• Women are born with a finite ovarian reserve
• Fertility is influenced by several factors, including age, egg quality, hormones, genetics, and overall ovarian health
• Current evidence does not support reducing menstrual frequency as an established way to preserve fertility
• Research in this area is ongoing and is not part of routine fertility care today

An important question researchers continue to study is:

Can aspects of reproductive aging eventually be better understood or influenced in the future?

At present, there is no established treatment shown to extend fertility lifespan simply by reducing periods.

It is also important to remember that menstrual health, ovulation, hormone balance, and overall wellbeing are interconnected.

For women with:
• fertility concerns
• ovarian cysts
• endometriosis
• low AMH

an individualized discussion and fertility assessment may help guide informed decisions.

Some exercises may feel different when living with Adenomyosis

Exercise is often encouraged for overall health and wellbeing, but every woman’s experience with Adenomyosis can be different.

Some women report that certain activities may be associated with symptoms such as:
• bloating
• pelvic heaviness
• cramps
• fatigue
• increased discomfort during flare phases

This does not mean exercise is harmful. Factors such as symptom patterns, pelvic floor tension, inflammation, and individual comfort levels may influence how the body responds.

During symptomatic phases, some women may find gentler activities more comfortable, such as:
• walking
• mobility exercises
• restorative yoga
• breathing practices
• guided pelvic health exercises

Movement is not one-size-fits-all, and what feels supportive can vary from person to person.

If pelvic symptoms are affecting your daily life or exercise routine, speaking with a healthcare professional may help guide the next steps.

Many women experience painful or heavy periods and assume it is a normal part of life.

Sometimes, these symptoms may be linked to conditions like adenomyosis, which can often go unrecognized in the early stages.

Symptoms such as increasing menstrual pain, heavy bleeding, pelvic discomfort, or a feeling of heaviness should not be ignored.

A timely gynecological evaluation can help identify the possible cause and guide women toward appropriate management options based on their individual health needs.

PCOS is often misunderstood.

And now, many experts are reconsidering the name itself.

Why?

Because “Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome” does not fully explain what many women actually experience.

Many women with PCOS may not even have ovarian cysts. Instead, they struggle with:
• irregular periods
• acne and hair growth
• weight fluctuations
• insulin resistance
• fatigue
• fertility concerns

This is why the term PMOS (PolyMetabolic Ovarian Syndrome) is entering medical conversations.

The condition is not just about the ovaries. It is closely linked to metabolism, hormones, inflammation, and long-term health.

Early diagnosis and structured treatment can make a significant difference.

If you are experiencing persistent cycle irregularities or hormonal symptoms, do not ignore them.

Are GLP-1 medications like Ozempic affecting your periods or fertility?

GLP-1 medications (such as Ozempic and Mounjaro) are increasingly used for weight management and metabolic health. Some women may notice changes in their menstrual cycle or ovulation patterns after starting these treatments.

Here’s what is commonly observed:

• Improved insulin sensitivity may support more regular cycles in some women with PCOS
• Ovulation may resume, which can increase the chance of natural conception
• Absorption of oral contraceptive pills may vary, especially during dose adjustments
• These medications support metabolic health but are not a cure for PCOS
• They are not recommended during pregnancy and should be used under medical guidance

Every individual responds differently.

If you’ve noticed changes in your cycle after starting GLP-1 therapy, it’s important to discuss this with a qualified specialist.
